It would mean being the easiest Fox to deceive, the one who let herself be carried away by an illusion and returned with her tail between her legs. 

No! I had to rebuild myself. Without my father's protection. Without his money. Without his name as a shield. I had to prove to myself, and to him, that I could survive despite everything. 

“I must admit that in your… sociological analysis… you’re not entirely wrong,” I lied, crossing my arms over my chest, trying to hide the trembling of my hands. “But that doesn’t mean I’m desperate. I still have options.” 

“If you say so…” he murmured, picking up his glass again and finishing the rest of the whiskey. His eyes flashed with a glint that told me he was about to make his final offer. “Look, Doctor. I’m offering you a one-year marriage. A year in which you’ll have every perk you could want, plus prestige. If money is your concern, I assure you your bank account will be the last thing on your mind. If you want a job, I can get you a position at the best pediatric hospital in the city with a single phone call. If you want that man’s wife, Henry, to never breathe near you again, I’ll make sure she disappears from your life completely. Ask me for anything you want, as long as you accept.” 

The offer was tempting. More than tempting, it was almost indecent in its generosity. Mainly because it would cleanse my dignity, my reputation. Not be anyone's mistress. Being the wife of a powerful man, even if it was a charade, would give me the time and the shield I needed to rebuild my career and my life. 

The rest—the money, the position at the hospital—I could acquire it myself eventually. But the protection and status he offered were immediate. 

"In exchange for what?" I asked, my voice now firmer, straightening my back and looking him directly in the eyes. There was no trace of Dr. Giraffe in me now. I was Zara Fox, negotiating her future. "What is it that a man like you, who seems to have everything, needs from me?" I didn't buy the story of a simple marriage. 

He paused for a moment before answering. The strategic gleam in his eyes softened slightly, replaced by a shadow of vulnerability that surprised me. The way his voice softened, becoming almost soothing, touched me deeply. 

"In exchange for making my daughter happy." 

My heart skipped a beat. I hadn't expected that. I expected him to ask me to be his trophy at charity dinners, to warm his bed, to be a silent companion. But to make Alina happy? 

"And how do you expect me to do that?" I asked, without thinking, genuine confusion in my voice. "Happiness isn't something you can buy." 

"Doctor… I'm a very realistic man," he said, his tone becoming practical and curt again. "I know forcing you to give Alina genuine affection is impossible. But I can ask you to take care of her. To be a mother to her. To go shopping with her, to take her to school, to tell her those giraffe stories she loved so much in London. One year of being the perfect mother to her. A year of sham marriage, yes, but a year in which my daughter would have a stable mother figure."

I didn't know whether to laugh or cry at the desperate, almost pathetic way in which this man, who seemed to pull the strings in the city, wanted to buy his daughter's happiness. 

His words sounded somewhat unreal, almost fantastical, as if he believed that a wife for hire could heal a child's wounds. But then I remembered little Alina's face in the hospital. Those big blue eyes, like her father's, filled with a silent pain, a loneliness that no amount of toys or luxuries seemed able to fill. 

"Why are you asking this of me?" I asked, my voice now soft. "There must be hundreds of women in this city who would accept this deal without hesitation, just for the money and the status. Why me?" 

He looked at me with brutal honesty. 

"I'll be honest with you, Doctor. In London, I noticed the affinity she showed for you" he paused briefly before continuing "My daughter has a problem: she doesn't speak. She's already been evaluated by the best neurologist and a renowned child psychologist. It's not a physical condition; she's silent by choice. She lives locked in her own world, one made of silence. And today, a doctor repeated something I've been hearing for years: what Alina needs... is a mother."

My heart ached at the image of little Alina locked in her silence, suffering a grief that no one could fully understand. 

As a pediatrician, I had seen many cases of children who reacted to trauma or loss with mutism. It was a defense mechanism, a way to protect themselves from the pain of the outside world. 

"May I ask… where is her mother?" I exclaimed, my voice barely a whisper. I knew I was treading on dangerous ground, but I needed to understand. 

His expression changed instantly. Coldness returned to his face, but this time it was mixed with a contained fury that made me shudder. His eyes became icy blades. 

"She doesn't have a mother," he said, his voice harsh, sharp as glass. 

“We all come from one, sir,” I replied, my voice calm but firm. I wasn’t going to be intimidated by his bad mood. “If we’re going to make a deal, I need honesty. I can’t be a mother to your daughter if I don’t know what happened to the previous one.” 

The look he gave me was almost deadly. I felt he was about to throw me out of his apartment, to cancel the deal before it even began. But I didn’t move. I stood looking at him, holding his gaze with a determination that, for the first time, seemed to surprise him. 

“If you don’t tell me, then I’ll leave…” I said, getting up simply from the sofa, ready to walk out the door and face my fate alone. 

But before I could take a step, I felt his hand close around my wrist. His grip was firm, possessive, but not painful. He pulled me down, silently demanding that I sit back down. His eyes were locked on mine, a battle of wills he clearly wasn't about to lose. 

"Fine," he grunted, releasing my wrist and sitting back down, running a hand through his hair in frustration. His mask of coldness had cracked slightly. "Alina's mother... died when she was born." 

Now I could understand that pain, that despair I saw in his eyes when he spoke of his daughter. He wasn't just a rich father trying to buy an easy solution. He was a broken man, trying to mend what fate had shattered. 

I looked at him with genuine understanding. My heart softened a little toward this arrogant and insufferable man. 

"I'm so sorry for your loss, sir," I said, patting his hand in an instinctive gesture of comfort. "I'm truly sorry. It's a terrible tragedy." 

I quickly withdrew my hand, realizing how bold I'd been. I resumed my professional posture. 

"I... accept the deal. I agree to be Alina's mother for a year. I agree to pretend to have a perfect marriage. But I have my own conditions." 

He looked at me curiously. 

"I'm all ears, Dr. Giraffe..." 

"First, you'll help me hide from my father. I ran away from home in London, and I don't want to go back looking like a loser, much less hear 'I told you so' from him. I want to prove to myself that I can make it on my own, even with a broken heart. You have the power and the resources to make me invisible to him." 

He nodded slowly, a brazen, calculating smile spreading across his face. 

"Don't worry about that," he exclaimed. "If you marry me, you'll take my last name. I assure you, you'll have more prestige and security than you've ever known. Besides," he added, leaning forward, "you won't need to work this year. Not if you don't want to. Believe me, I'll be an excellent provider. Your wish is my command." 

Sexist! The word echoed in my mind. It sounded so easy for a man like him. He believed that with money and power he could buy anything, even my ambitions. 

"Look, sir," I said, my tone icy, crossing my arms again. "I want to resume my medical residency here in New York and finish my specialization in pediatrics. Do you understand? I'm not a trophy to be displayed in a glass case. I'm a professional woman." 

He let out a laugh, a husky, genuine sound that resonated in the luxurious apartment. He leaned back on the sofa, looking at me with a mixture of amusement and a new kind of respect. 

"Well... the little giraffe can be a lioness when she wants to. How interesting," he commented ironically, a flicker of challenge in his eyes. "I like that way of thinking. I don't object, but I should clarify that working with me won't be necessary." 

My eyes narrowed. I didn't like his superior tone. 

"What I'm telling you is true, sir. So don't expect a submissive, kept wife from me. Believe me, your money is the last thing on my mind. I have my own plans." 

He let out another laugh, this time lower, more husky, almost dangerous. He leaned forward once more, his face inches from mine.

"In my world, little lioness..." he said, his voice dropping to a seductive and terrifying whisper, "everyone has a price. Absolutely everyone. It's just a matter of finding the right currency." 

"Not in my case," I replied, my voice firm. "So, if you want this contract, it'll be like this: you give me absolute protection, you help me finish my specialization, and I'll be the best mother Alina could ever wish for. A year of pretense, yes. But a year of professional pretense. Do we have a deal?"

V 6. My Fiancée

Julian Mackenzie's POV 

The giraffe doctor's overly defensive attitude struck me as comical. She was so different from all the women I'd ever met. Not even Lia had that innocent air about her that this woman possessed. 

What she was asking was easy for me. I was even more than willing to lend a hand to make her degree and US residency official. 

"Of course," I said, taking her hand to seal the deal. 

Her smile shifted from sweet to wicked. It was quick, but I noticed. 

"Then it's best if the contract is drawn up, and I request that a few conditions be added." 

Her trying to negotiate with me was even funnier. I could see she had a strong personality, but even when she was angry, she looked like a little lion cub. 

"Fine, you can add your conditions. We'll do that tomorrow in my office. For now, I'll take you to your hotel. You can even stay in this apartment until we get married,” I told her. 

She looked around, not entirely convinced. I didn’t quite understand why she was so analytical, even as soon as she walked in, until she spoke: 

“No, I won’t be staying here.”

 Those were her first words. I didn’t understand why. After all, this apartment was luxurious. Wasn’t she used to luxury? 

“Can I know the reason for your refusal?” 

“Well, I’m not going to stay in a womanizer’s den. God only knows how many women have set foot in this place.” 

I hadn’t expected that reaction, much less the way she said it. It was true that many women had been here, but I didn’t consider myself a womanizer. I had always been upfront about my affairs. 

“Don’t you think this way of criticizing me is very aggressive?” I asked. 

“It’s not criticism, it’s reality. I have a brother, and I know very well what men like him do in places like this. So I won’t be staying here.” 

"It's true, I'm no saint, but I'm not a womanizer either. Fine, if the young lady doesn't want to stay here, we'll find somewhere else to stay." 

"Okay, but I think it would be best if you dropped me off at my hotel. I'm tired; it's been a difficult day." 

"Alright, Dr. Giraffe… I'll take you to your hotel." 

"Zara… my name is Zara, not Dr. Giraffe. Is that clear?" 

I smiled at her words. Zara… it was a name that suited her very well. 

"Okay, Zara. My name is Julian." 

She smiled and said without hesitation: 

"A very nice name for a very cold man," she commented as she stood up and walked toward the door to leave. 

"A very direct woman," I thought. 

I took her to the address she gave me. When I saw the area, I raised my eyebrows. 

“Are you really that short of money that you have to stay in a place like this?” 

She looked back at me and said, “It’s all I can pay in cash. If I use my cards, my father will be able to track me down.” 

She talked so much about her father that I was starting to wonder if he was a possessive, controlling lunatic. 

I parked the car and got out to walk her there. As we entered the lobby, she turned back to me: 

“You can go now, Julián. I can walk from here on my own.” 

“Leave you here? Impossible. From today on, you’re officially my fiancée, and nothing you say will change my mind. You don’t want to stay in my apartment, I accept that, but I’ll put you up in a better hotel.” 

I owned stock in a well-known hotel chain. I wasn’t just a successful lawyer; I also had a couple of other businesses. 

“It’s not necessary,” she replied. 

It wasn’t an option. I didn’t even ask. 

“It’s for your safety. For your peace of mind, I'll reserve it in my name, okay?" 

I was grateful she didn't make it any harder for me… she finally nodded. I took the key from her hand and practically dragged her to her room. She had a small suitcase. 

I took it and we left. 

I had a presidential suite—it was one of the perks for members—and I gave it to her. 

"You'll be more comfortable here, Zara," I said as I left, once she'd settled in. 

"Thank you, Julián," she replied politely. 

We were standing face to face. She was an elegant woman, tall, yes, but even in the heels she was wearing, she didn't reach me. I was 6'3" and she was, at most, 5'9". Her head almost touched my chin. 

"I'll come for you tomorrow. We'll go for breakfast and I'll take you to my office to finalize our agreement." 

"Okay. Get some rest." 

“Do you have a number I can call you on?” I asked. 

“No, my cell phone is off, and I haven’t gotten a new line yet.” 

“Okay. Just don’t move from here. We’ll take care of everything tomorrow.” 

She nodded. I turned around and left. 

I drove straight home. It was very late when I arrived. My father was still waiting for me in the living room. 

“Son, it’s very late.” 

“I know, Dad,” I said, loosening my tie and sighing. “I had a strange day today.” 

“Strange? Why?” 

“Because today, Dad, I found the woman who will be Alina’s mother.”

“What are you talking about?” he asked. 

“That I found her, Dad. I found the perfect woman to be Alina’s mother and my wife.”

"Julian, do you really know what you're talking about?" 

"Yes, Dad. I'm getting married." 

"Julian, marriage isn't a joke. Are you sure? What happened to all those times you told me you didn't believe in love? Son, I don't want you to get hurt like that woman did... Irina." 

The mention of Alina's mother filled me with the same fury I'd felt since she told me she was going to have an abortion. 

Irina Valkova. The woman I buried in my heart, the one who made me stop believing in love. 

I swore I'd never love again. It was pointless. But in my family, love was important, so I wasn't about to tell them that this woman I was marrying was just a well-made arrangement. 

"Dad, that's all in the past. Zara is lovely, and Alina feels comfortable with her." 

"Alina? Has she met her?" he asked. 

“Yes, Dad, and you will too. She’s not from this country; I met her in London. So, in order for her to live here, we’ll have a civil ceremony soon, and the church wedding will be in a year.” 

I lied to him. This was the second lie of the day. Not typical of me. I might be a scoundrel, but never a liar. And today I crossed that line. 

I lied to Zara when I told her Alina’s mother had died, and now to my father, who had always been my confidant, talking about Zara as if I truly loved her. 

“That’s fine, son. From what you’re saying, she’s a very interesting woman.” 

More than interesting, I repeated to myself. 

She’ll be the key to my daughter’s happiness. 

“Yes, Dad. Let’s get some rest.” I escorted him to his room and then sought refuge in my little girl’s. 

She slept in absolute peace, oblivious to the wounds I carry in my soul and the trail of ashes I had to leave behind to have her with me today. 

Because only the day I held her in my arms for the first time—small, fragile, mine—did I feel my heart begin to beat again after so long dormant. 

Now, the path has closed behind me. There is no turning back. I will marry; I will sign a contract, seal a pact, and surrender my freedom for a single purpose: her happiness.

VI 7. Old?

Julian Mackenzie's POV 

The next day, the sun was barely beginning to paint the sky when I was already up. My exercise routine wasn't just for vanity; it was the only way to release the tension built up from what awaited me. 

After a quick shower, I slipped into one of my tailored suits. The cut was perfect, accentuating my shoulders with the precision that only money and good taste can buy. 

In the kitchen, the aroma of coffee and pancakes filled the air as I prepared breakfast for Alina. It's my favorite ritual, the only moment of the day when the world shrinks to my daughter's smile. 

She appears in her school uniform, a whirlwind of energy, and gives me a kiss. Her blue eyes, a carbon copy of mine, shine with that light that only innocence can give. My parents and my grandfather Bruce join us at the table. The smell of home gives me a false sense of peace. 

"Family, I have a surprise. I'm taking you out to dinner tonight. I want you to meet someone very special." 

Alina looks at me curiously, her eyebrows arched in a silent question. 

"Baby, I know you're going to love it," I say, stroking her cheek. "Your grandparents are picking you up today. I have things to do, but I'll see you tonight." 

She nods, reassured, and smiles. 

"Julian, what's this all about?" My mother's voice cuts through the familiar atmosphere, that tone that's known all my lies since I was old enough to understand. 

"Relax, Mom," I say, getting up and straightening my shirt cuffs. "I'll just say that I listened to your advice." 

I wink at her and leave before she can ask any more questions. The echo of her doubts fades as I close the door. 

It's eight in the morning. Zara must be waiting for me.

I arrive at the hotel with an iron will. I order the manager to bring breakfast up to my suite. I don't know her tastes, so I order everything. A calculated excess. This is my territory, and I want her to know it from the first bite. 

I knock on the door. When she opens it, my pulse quickens. It's not a reaction I can control, but one I won't admit aloud either. 

Zara is perfectly dressed. A dress that clings to her curves, her hair pulled back in a ponytail that reveals her neck, elegant and fragile at the same time. 

"Good morning, Zara." 

"Good morning, Julian," her voice is as soft as silk. 

I made my way into the room without waiting for an invitation. Dominating the space was part of my nature. 

"I ordered breakfast. How about we eat and then go to my office?" 

She nods, a minimal but firm movement. However, when the waiter entered with the excessive number of trays, Zara rolled her eyes with an elegance that I found both irritating and fascinating. 

"Don't you think this is an excessive amount of food?" she asked, raising an eyebrow. 

I shrugged, leaning against the window frame to get a better look at her.

"No," I replied, shrugging as I sat down. "I didn't know what you liked, so I ordered everything on the menu." 

I sat down in one of the chairs facing the small table and gestured to the one opposite with a slight nod: an order disguised as an invitation. 

"Come, sit down and enjoy." 

"Thank you," she said, moving with that distinctly British grace. 

She looked young, too young. If I hadn't met her in the hospital, I would have sworn she wasn't even of legal age yet. She has a sweet air about her, yes. But also a quiet determination. 

"Zara." 

"Yes?" 

"How old are you?" Curiosity got the better of me. 

"I recently turned twenty-six. And you?" 

"I'll be thirty-six in two months," I replied, and for the first time in my life, feeling that ten-year age difference weighed heavily on my chest. 

"Wow... you're old," she remarked with a nonchalance that struck a blow to my ego. 

The word stings. No one, absolutely no one, has ever called me old in my life. 

"Old?" I paused before adding, "My father is ten years older than my mother and he's never looked old next to her," I retorted, my voice dropping an octave, laden with that possessive virility. "The men in my family are very... vigorous. My grandfather married my grandmother when he was twenty years older." 

She let out a laugh that broke the tension. 

“You don’t need to explain,” she said, regaining her composure with a speed that made me doubt my own judgment. “In a marriage of convenience, age isn’t important. After all, we’ll be free in a year.” 

dmn it, she was right. Why was I justifying my age? 

“That’s true. So, if you’re finished, let’s go. We have a lot to do,” I said, regaining my composure. 

We arrived at my office in record time. My secretary, a woman I trusted completely, who had seen me climb every rung of my career as a lawyer, greeted us with a surprised smile at seeing me accompanied, since I've never brought a woman here who isn't a family member.

I gestured for Zara to take a seat in the chair across from my mahogany desk, while I sank into my leather armchair, reclaiming my territory. 

Susan looked at us, bewildered; I suppose that seeing Zara, a complete stranger, sitting across from my desk as if she were born to be there, must feel like the end of the world. 

"Susan, no one is to interrupt us," I ordered. 

She nodded and left. 

"Let's clarify the terms," ​​I began, crossing my fingers on the desk. "I've drafted the basic clauses, but I want to add a crucial one: if my daughter shows the slightest sign of discomfort with you, the contract is null and void. Immediate divorce, regardless of how much time has passed." I exclaimed, making it clear that my daughter was untouchable. 

"I understand," Zara replied, unfazed. "That sounds perfect. But I also have a couple of clauses to add." 

I look at her with a wry smile. So now the giraffe doctor has demands? 

"Go ahead," I replied, leaning back in my chair, expecting some absurd financial request. 

Forgetting that Zara wasn't like the others. 

She leans slightly forward, and suddenly the air in the office becomes thick. 

"Julian, marriage is a serious commitment. Even if it's by contract, I want it to be handled with seriousness. Number one: we're going to make it a rule that, at least three nights a week, you have dinner with Alina and me. You'll also be obligated to take us on a trip once a month. My father, no matter how much work he had, was always there for us, and we were his priority. I want to give your daughter that example, the same one I grew up with." 

I remain silent, assessing her. It's not a request. It's a sentence. 

“Number two,” she continued, her voice firm, “as your wife, you will respect my place both in public and in private. And by that, I mean you will commit to being faithful to this contract and the marriage bond we are about to enter into. You understand, right? That your ‘nighttime adventures’ end for the duration of our marriage?” 

My blood boils, but not with anger. With disbelief. Does this little girl intend to set limits for me? 

I lean forward, resting my elbows on the desk, my gaze hardening. 

“I understand the fidelity,” I said, my voice a low whisper. “But I will add a condition. You will fulfill your role as a wife. Both in public… and in private.”

Zara Fox's POV 

The Fox Family believes in predestined love with the same faith as we believe in God. 

In my family, love isn't something you search for; it simply arrives. 

And I had waited twenty-six years. Twenty-six years of hearing my mother say, "When it's your turn, Zara, you'll just know." Twenty-six years of feeling like my heart was an empty operating room waiting for the right surgeon.

The plane landed in New York with a slight jolt. 

Outside, the city bustled, oblivious to my arrival. 

I clutched my phone to my chest; it was still off. It had been like that for almost eight hours, since the plane took off from London, and I knew that if I turned it on, I'd find over a hundred missed calls from my father, Asher Fox, and several messages from my mother that would say something like: 

"Zara, please talk to us. Don't do anything you'll regret." 

Too late for that. 

For the first time in my life, I had disobeyed my father. For the first time in twenty-six years, I stopped being the girl who ate her vegetables without complaint, the one who got straight A's, the one who patiently waited for fate to deliver love on a silver platter. 

Now I'm in New York. I've left everything behind for a man I've known for two months. For a man who kissed me once on a rooftop and then had to return to his country. 

He's a cardiovascular surgeon, a New Yorker visiting London for a three-month mini-residency. I was on my pediatric ER rotation. Our paths crossed in one hallway, then another, then in the cafeteria, then in my dreams. 

The kiss came like an unexpected diagnosis: suddenly, without warning, and without any possibility of refusal. 

"I can't stop thinking about you, Dr. Zara Fox," he said against my lips, and his New York accent transformed my name into something I'd never heard before. Something that sounded like a promise. 

I, who had never been in love, surrendered in that instant. 

I didn't tell him I was coming. I wanted it to be a surprise. 

The taxi dropped me off right where Henry had told me he lived when he drew me a map on a paper napkin during our last coffee. 

“If you ever come to New York,” he said, his hand brushing against mine on the table, “this is where you’ll find me.” 

I put the napkin away. I still have it. Crumpled, with a coffee stain in the corner. 

The building was elegant. 

I rang the doorbell of his apartment, my fingers trembling. In my other hand, the suitcase containing my entire life for the next three months. 

The door opened. 

And the universe, that accomplice my family had trusted for generations, showed me its true face. 

It wasn’t Henry who answered. It was a woman. A woman with dark hair pulled back in a messy bun, wearing a man’s shirt—his shirt, I recognized the cut, the brand he used to wear—and a steaming cup of coffee between her fingers. 

On her left hand, a wedding ring caught the New York sunlight and threw it directly into my eyes. 

“Yes?” She said, raising an eyebrow. 

My brain, trained to assess patients in seconds, processed the information with a speed I both appreciated and hated. 

“I’m looking for Henry Black,” I said, holding her gaze with a certainty that brooked no doubt. 

The woman slowly looked up. Her eyes scanned my face, then down to the suitcase beside me, and back again, more attentive. 

“Who’s looking for him?” she asked, this time with a hint of caution in her voice. 

I gently gripped the suitcase handle, without looking away.

“Zara Fox,” I replied. 

“Ah,” she said, and her mouth curved into something that wasn’t a smile. "You're little Dr. Fox, aren't you?"

Little Dr.?

The word hit me like a ton of bricks. It wasn’t the title I had worked so hard to earn; I wasn't Dr. Fox, as my patients call me. Nor was I Zara, the name reserved for those who care for me. I was "little doctor." 

A diminutive. A term of contempt. A label. 

She knew who I was. 

Henry appeared behind her at that moment, his torso bare, his hair disheveled, his expression shifting from sleepiness to panic in less than a second. The three of us stared at each other in the doorway, forming a triangle with me at the other vertex. He opened his mouth. Closed it. Opened it again, unsure how to speak. 

And in his eyes, I saw something that broke me more than his shirt draped over her shoulders, more than the wedding ring, more than the word "little doctor." 

I saw a hint of calculation in his gaze. 

He wasn't afraid of having hurt me. He was assessing how much damage I could inflict on him. On his reputation. On his marriage. On his career. The scholarship he won in London depended, in part, on my father's connections. 

My father. 

The man I disobeyed for the first time in my life. For this. For a d'mnd lying man. 

"Zara," he finally said, and the sound of my name on his lips tasted like infected stitches. "This isn't what it looks like." 

At that moment, his wife let out a short laugh that sounded like bone breaking. 

"Seriously, Henry? You're going to do this? You're going to look her in the face and lie?" 

She turned to me and this time she did smile. A smile that pierced me. 

"I'll tell you what it is, little doctor..." She paused, then continued with contempt. "You're a means to an end. A lever. He never loved you. He was interested in your last name. Your father's connections. The letter of recommendation your uncle can sign. You were the consolation prize, the backup plan in case he couldn't get what he wanted the right way."

Something inside me broke. 

Henry's wife looked me up and down, assessing the damage with satisfaction. 

"Get out. You were the easiest Fox to fool..." she spat, each word landing on her finger. "And I'm warning you: don't you ever go near my husband again." 

Her eyes scanned my face with contempt before she added, almost in a venomous whisper: 

"Unless you want to keep behaving like what you already are. A homewrecker... A common mistress." 

The door slammed in my face. 

And with it... everything I thought was real. 

The stupidest mistake of my life wasn't getting on that plane. It was looking at Henry Black and swearing, with blind and ridiculous faith, that my destiny lay there... when in reality it was the abyss disguised as a promise.

I 2. A stranger

Zara Fox's POV 

With a shattered heart and my dignity reduced to ashes, I wandered aimlessly, trapped by the echo of my own mistakes. I couldn't understand when my dreams had been trampled: I abandoned London, my home; I left behind my family, my pride, everything that defined me… for a man who turned out to be married, and then discovered that he never truly loved me, that he only used me as a means to climb the ladder. 

The worst part is that my father was right. Because he had warned me. 

"You don't know that man, Zara. You know nothing about him." 

And I, for the first time, hadn't listened, hadn't wanted to. 

I went into a modest hotel in downtown New York. Nothing luxurious, just enough to blend in. I paid in cash; I knew my father too well. If I used one of my cards, he'd find me without any trouble. 

And at that moment, the last thing I needed was for Mr. Asher Fox to appear with his cold certainty and say, "I told you so." 

That was my only consolation: at least, for now, my father didn't know where I was. 

At some point, hunger won out over pride. 

I forced myself out onto the street, aimlessly, without knowing exactly what I was looking for. I knew nothing… except one thing: if I didn't eat something soon, I was going to faint and end up in a New York hospital, the last place I wanted to be. 

It was already late, so, as I wandered, I found a restaurant with bar service; just what I needed, because the only thing that could help me feel less miserable was a good meal. 

I went in and sat at a table for two, next to a beautiful window. 

The waiter handed me the menu and, with a thoughtful look, asked if I was feeling well. I looked at him, smiled… and replied, lying: 

“Yes, perfectly.” 

He nodded and took my order. 

The food was delicious. Afterward, the waiter invited me to the bar area. I nodded; a drink wouldn't be bad, I thought. I accepted and followed him. 

The bar was elegant, and the cocktail was impeccable. Honestly, I was starting to feel better. 

Suddenly, the air grew heavier, an invisible force compelled me to look at the person about to cross the threshold. 

A tall, blond man with intense blue eyes approached with a presence that was hard to ignore. I didn't know why he seemed familiar… until he turned toward the bar and the light fell on his hands. 

Yes. His hands. 

I recognized them before I recognized his face. I had seen them just a few days before, in London, at the private hospital where I was doing my residency. 

That morning. In the emergency room, where I worked my last shift before boarding the plane. 

A man had come in carrying a little girl, about five years old, in his arms. She had a fever, she was scared… and her eyes were the same deep blue as his. 

The little girl clung to his neck, convinced it was the only stable thing in a world crumbling around her. 

And he… 

He held her with those hands that I now saw cradling a glass of amber liqueur. Large, firm, almost rough hands… and yet, capable of a tenderness that completely belied the coldness of his expression. 

That detail didn't escape my notice. 

I had treated that little girl. 

"Alina," I whispered her name. I had heard it before, when a nurse was checking her charts. So, while I tried to bring her fever down with cold compresses, I stayed by her side, making up a silly story about giraffes who couldn't sleep unless they saw the stars. Now, remembering it, that moment returned with a soft, almost warm clarity. 

He introduced himself as the father. He listened to my diagnosis without interrupting, nodded once, and left without saying thank you. 

I don't usually remember faces. In the ER, faces become an indistinct sea. But that night… it wasn't his face that stayed with me. 

It was only his hands. 

And the way he, despite everything, held his daughter as if she were made of glass. 

He wasn't wearing a wedding ring either. Not a single mark on his skin to indicate that he'd ever worn one. 

Now he was there, three stools away, drinking slowly, his gaze lost somewhere that didn't belong in that bar. 

Before I could think about it too much, I got up. 

The impulse drew me to him. 

"Excuse me…" I said, stopping beside him. 

He turned his head slowly; any interruption seemed like an annoyance he assessed before tolerating it. His eyes rested on me without recognition, without warmth, only with a cold evaluation. 

"Yes?" he said neutrally. 

Nothing. 

Not a spark. Not a trace of memory. 

I felt a strange emptiness in my chest. Ridiculous, considering we had barely exchanged a few words days before. Even so, I opened my mouth, ready to remind him and ask about the little girl's health. 

"I'm the doctor who treated your daughter…" 

I didn't finish the sentence. 

The door opened again, and this time she walked in.

Henry's wife. 

I recognized her instantly. She was now wearing a perfectly tailored red dress and flawless makeup that made her look like a model off a magazine cover. 

What was she doing there? 

I didn't know. 

But there she was, in the company of another woman. 

She noticed me, strode toward me with determined steps and a blazing gaze: 

"Do you really think you can come to my house?" she spat, her voice dripping with venom. "That you can come to my city and try to steal my husband from me?" 

The waiter vanished. The ambient sound died away. Even the man next to me froze, her attention completely captivated. 

I froze too. That woman was out of control. 

"Do you know how pathetic you are?" she continued, moving closer until she was invading my space. "My husband only used you." 

Every word hit its mark. Hearing them speak aloud, there, exposed and n8ked in front of strangers… 

It was as if my skin were being ripped off. 

I knew exactly what she expected: for me to break down, to cry, to run away. 

But something inside me—something tired of losing—refused. 

My hand, gripping the edge of the bar, loosened. It moved. And before I could stop myself, it closed around the wrist of the man beside me. 

His skin was warm. His pulse, firm and steady. Even so, I felt it tense at my touch. 

He turned his face slightly toward me, surprised by the intrusion… by the audacity. 

And then I spoke. 

“I think what you’re thinking is a big misunderstanding,” I said, looking directly at Henry’s wife. My voice was firm, calm, pretending not to crumble inside. "Let me make it clear that Henry isn't the reason I came to this country." 

I barely squeezed his wrist under my fingers. 

"The real reason is him..." I exclaimed, looking at the stranger, adding, "...my boyfriend...the man I'm going to marry." 

The silence was absolute. 

I felt the stranger freeze, trapped in that moment where he had to decide whether to back away...or play along. 

The woman blinked, bewildered. 

"With him?" she asked, incredulous. "You're going to marry a complete stranger to save your pride?" 

Her laugh was brief. Cruel, pure mockery. 

"It's not pride, it's love," I replied. 

Hearing me speak, the man sat up straight enough to command respect effortlessly, without raising his voice, without losing that dangerous calm. 

"Ma'am," he said, each syllable falling like a sentence. "The fact that your husband is a pathological liar doesn't give you the right to make a scene by defaming my fiancée." 

He didn't let go of me. Nor did I. 

He turned slightly toward me. His eyes assessed me again, but this time there was something different. "Interest." 

He raised an eyebrow, almost imperceptibly. 

And then, with a nonchalance that disarmed me more than anything else, he said: 

"Shall we go, my love?" 

He held out his hand. 

"We have a wedding to plan." 

Henry's wife's mouth fell open. The waiter dropped a glass. The owner let out a low whistle. 

His fingers closed around mine with a firmness that wasn't tenderness. 

It felt like a pact. 

Without knowing it, I was about to sign the most dangerous contract of my life. 

Not with a man who would lie to me. 

But with one that would make me forget what it felt like to be broken.

II 3. Use my last name for real

Julian Mackenzie's POV 

LOVE… That word is reserved only for my daughter, my princess, my everything: Alina. 

I know. My grandfather Bruce clings to life just for her. He worries that, over the years, I haven't been able to give her a mother. But no woman is worthy of that title. 

My mother tried to make me understand once, when she told me: 

"She needs a mother, son. Just like you, when you were a child, needed a father. I know the circumstances are different… But please, try your best to find a good woman." 

That's my karma. I'm aware that I hurt a good woman like Lia. And I've paid dearly for that mistake. 

What consumes me now is my daughter. She doesn't speak. 

A few days ago, I took her to London to see Alistair Fox, a friend of my father's, a world-renowned neurologist. After evaluating her, he determined that there was nothing wrong with her. 

That day, my daughter suffered a sudden and alarming fever. Her little body was burning up, and within hours her temperature rose uncontrollably, forcing me to rush her to the hospital. There, a young doctor with a calm voice explained that her immune system was weakened. 

I barely paid attention. I was annoyed by how casually my daughter snuggled into her arms as she told her a ridiculous giraffe story. 

Now, in the waiting room of Manhattan's best child psychologist, I wait for my daughter to be seen. Alistair recommended therapy, and I followed his advice. 

The door opens. 

"Mr. Mackenzie, please come in," the psychologist says, as her assistant takes Alina away with the promise of a treat. 

I enter, feeling a bit anxious. 

"Get to the point. Tell me what's wrong with my daughter." 

The woman confronts me with a professional calm that irritates me. 

"Since you ask... your daughter needs a mother figure. In kindergarten, she observes her classmates and associates that emptiness with silence. It's not that she can't speak, Mr. Mackenzie. She simply doesn't want to." 

Again. Always the same conclusion. She needs a mother. 

"She has my sisters, my mother... Aren't they enough as mother figures?" I ask, my jaw clenched. 

"They fill the role of an aunt, a grandmother. You must understand that everyone processes their needs differently. Alina needs to know about her origins. She needs to fill that void." 

I've never denied her origins. But if I have to invent a mother for her, I will. The thought forms in my mind like a cold, calculated plan. 

"I understand, Doctor. I hope that with your work you can help my daughter." 

"Of course, Mr. Mackenzie. We'll take it slowly, although I admit your daughter is quite closed off." 

 A shiver of fury runs through me. 

"Don't blame my daughter for your ineptitude," I exclaimed angrily. 

I leave without giving her time to reply. I pick up my princess and carry her home. 

"Are you okay?" I ask her. 

She just nods, burying her face in my neck. 

I'm fed up. My daughter's suffering hurts me more than my own. 

When I arrive, I find my parents and Grandpa Bruce visiting. At ninety years old, he's still traveling. All to see Alina. 

I feel overwhelmed. I need to escape their pitying and disappointed stares. I know I'm turning thirty-six, but I'm not the only man in the world without a steady partner. 

"Dad, I have to go. Take care of Alina, please." 

My father nods silently. I don't need to say anything more. 

Tonight I don't want a club or a woman to offer fleeting relief from my stress. I end up at my friend Jeremy's restaurant and bar. A drink won't hurt. 

As I walk in, my gaze instinctively falls upon a woman. Long, light hair, an elegance that suits the place. Yes, I admit it, I'm a jerk, because the first thing I notice is her hips, the shape of her buttocks, and the way she moves with a naturalness that promises more than just aesthetics. 

I sit at the bar, a couple of meters away from her. 

The bartender serves me my usual. Alina's face flashes through my mind, and frustration tightens in my chest. 

Then she gets up and walks toward me. I'm not in the mood for a one-night stand tonight, but maybe… maybe I can make an exception. 

The light from the bar illuminates her face, and my breath catches in my throat. 

I recognize her. It's the doctor from London. The one with the giraffes. 

I look at her sharply, feigning indifference. But she recognizes me and tries to speak. 

I pretend not to remember her, making it clear I have no interest. 

What happens next takes me by surprise. A woman bursts in, shouting insults I can't quite process. 

Her verbal aggressor calls her pathetic and even blames her for being with her husband, and a primal impulse is triggered within me. I don't know why it bothers me so much that this woman insults this stranger. But she does. 

When the doctor, in an act of desperation, blurts out: 

"He's my boyfriend! We're going to get married!" 

I freeze. Not because of the lie, but because of her audacity. Because of the way her fingers tremble as she holds my hand. 

I could push her away. It would be the logical thing to do. 

Instead, I stand up and take her hand. 

Her hand is soft, small. It fits perfectly in mine, as if it was meant to be there from the beginning. 

I lead her away without letting her speak, feeling the other woman's furious gaze behind us. I put her in my car. 

The pieces fall into place in my mind with terrifying clarity. This woman could be the answer to my problems. She's not just any woman. She… She's already been close to Alina, my daughter, who felt comfortable with her. 

She's a doctor, intelligent, and seems desperate. She's simply perfect. 

She lied to save herself. But I'll make her lie real. 

I climb into the driver's seat and, without a word, start the engine. 

The silence in the car is tense, heavy with questions she doesn't dare ask. 

I'm not going home. Not where my family is. I'm driving to the apartment I use for my casual encounters. It's private, discreet, and perfect for sealing a good deal. 

I park. I grip the steering wheel, my knuckles white. She looks at me, fear beginning to shine in her eyes. 

Finally, I speak, my voice a low whisper. 

"You said you were my girlfriend. You said we'd get married." 

She opens her mouth to explain, but I don't give her time. 

I spin in my seat, cornering her against the door. 

"I'm not a man who lets a woman use his name in vain. If you're going to use my last name, it has to be real. 

I glance down at her lips, which tremble slightly, and then into her eyes. My decision is made. It's not crazy. It's the most logical solution I've had in years. 

"We're going to get married," I declare, my voice firm, leaving no room for argument. "And you're going to be the mother of my daughter." 

Her face pales. I see panic reflected in her pupils, but also something else… a flicker of indignation struggling to surface. 

In my mind, there's only one voice repeating itself over and over, like a dark prayer: 

"Alina, my daughter… Daddy's finally going to give you a mother."

III 4. Doctor Giraffe 🦒

Zara Fox's POV 

dmn! New York was definitely overrun with lunatics, and I, with my luck, had run into two of the most dangerous specimens in a single day. 

First, Henry's wife, the man for whom I'd crossed the Atlantic, leaving the safety of my London home and defying my father's wrath, only to discover that his "bachelordom" included a furious wife ready to rip my head off. 

And now, him. 

The man walking beside me toward the elevator. I didn't know his name, only that he had a daughter with the saddest eyes in the world, hands capable of disarming a security guard with terrifying elegance, and a premarital proposal that sounded insane. 

The elevator doors opened directly onto a penthouse that screamed money, power, and an alarming lack of feminine touch. It was spectacular, I couldn't deny it. 

It was the quintessential sanctuary of a golden bachelor. I knew because my brother Zack's London apartment had the exact same "hunting ground" vibe. Zack used it exclusively to impress his conquests, and well, the rest is history. 

My instincts kicked in, going on high alert. The adrenaline that had kept me going during the altercation at the restaurant began to dissipate, giving way to an icy caution. 

If this man thought that, because he'd saved me from a humiliating scene, I was a damsel in distress willing to repay him with "sinful" favors, he was sorely mistaken. I'd rather die than become a stranger's trophy. 

He walked toward a built-in minibar. He moved with predatory grace, each step exuding a confidence that was starting to deeply irritate me. 

"Would you like something to drink?" he asked, his voice deep. He didn't even bother to look at me. 

"No, thank you." 

“I just want to know why the hll I’m here,” I replied, crossing my arms, trying to project a confidence I didn’t entirely feel. 

The man didn’t respond immediately. I watched him pour an amber liquid—probably an excessively expensive single malt whisky—into a cut-glass tumbler. 

This man was definitely an enigma. The version I’d seen at the hospital, kneeling before his daughter Alina, his voice breaking with anguish, seemed like a mirage compared to the block of coldness and arrogance I now faced. 

He turned and approached me. The ambient lighting highlighted the sharp angles of his face, a face that, under other circumstances, I would have found devastatingly attractive. 

He sat on the leather sofa opposite me, crossing one leg with an elegance that felt almost like an insult to my current state of emotional disarray. He took a slow sip, studying me with those deep, unfathomable blue eyes. 

“Look, Dr. Giraffe…” 

“Excuse me?” Indignation shot through me like an electric shock. 

Giraffe? Had he spared me one humiliation only to inflict another? 

“What did you call me?” 

He offered a tiny, almost imperceptible smile that didn’t reach his eyes. There was something cruel about that smile, something that told me he enjoyed provoking me. 

“I call you that because in London, at the hospital, I overheard you telling my daughter a story. It was about giraffes. I don’t know your real name, so for now, Dr. Giraffe seems fitting. You’re tall, blonde, and have that tender yet defensive quality those animals have. Besides,” he added, taking another sip of his whiskey and fixing his gaze on mine with an intensity that made me shift uncomfortably in my seat, “it’s quite curious how fate has brought us together again.” 

I gritted my teeth. So this man remembered me perfectly from London, and yet he had completely ignored me in the restaurant until he had no other choice. His arrogance was monumental. 

Nevertheless, I took a deep breath and decided to swallow my pride. He had helped me escape the restaurant unharmed, protecting me from Henry's wife's fury and the judgmental stares of the other diners. I owed him that. 

"Did you bring me here just to give me silly nicknames and bask in your good memory?" I replied, my tone icy. If he thought he was going to intimidate me with his opulence and steely gaze, he was sorely mistaken. I've dealt with worse men. I've dealt with my father. 

"All right. I'll get to the point," he said finally, his expression straightening, abandoning any trace of mocking amusement for a sharp, professional seriousness. It was like watching a predator switch from "play" mode to "hunt" mode. "While we were at the restaurant, I saw a very clear situation. You're an intelligent woman who made a stupid decision for a man who wasn't worth it. Now you desperately need a shield. You need a boyfriend, a husband, a commitment... anything to make that miserable man's wife leave you alone and give you back some of the dignity you lost." 

His words, though uttered with deceptive gentleness, struck me with the force of a punch. The truth hurt, and he was using it like a scalpel to dissect my situation. 

I hadn't knowingly gotten involved with a married man. Henry had lied to me. 

But in the eyes of the world, and especially in the eyes of his wife, I was the mistress. The home-wrecker. I felt a pang of vulnerability in my chest, but I refused to let him see my tears. I straightened my back, mirroring his posture, even though inside I felt like I was about to crumble. 

"Sir... I think there's a mistake in your analysis," I said, my voice trembling slightly despite my efforts to keep it steady. "I never knew Henry was married. I fell in love with him, yes. I believed his words and made the mistake of leaving everything behind—my career, my family, my country—for him. But I'm not a mistress. I was a fool, but not an accomplice." 

He nodded slowly, not sympathetically, but as if checking a box on a mental list. 

“I want to make it clear that I’m not one to judge your morality or your naiveté. That’s none of my business. What is my business is that, just as you need me right now to avoid being devoured alive by New York high society and a spiteful wife, I need you.” 

“What exactly do you mean?” I asked, my voice barely a whisper. 

He placed his glass of whiskey on the coffee table with a dry, decisive thud. He leaned forward, his face inches from mine. I could smell the aroma of his drink, mixed with an expensive, masculine cologne. His eyes were fixed on mine, with a determination that chilled me to the bone. 

“I want to offer you a marriage contract.” 

I felt the world stop spinning for a second. That D'mnd word. My grandfather had forced my grandmother into a marriage contract. My own father had bound my mother in the same way. And now, this man, this complete stranger who called me "Dr. Giraffe," wanted the same from me. It was unacceptable. 

"And what makes you think I would accept something like that? What makes you think I'm so desperate as to sell my freedom to a stranger?" 

He smiled again, but this time there was no mockery, only a cold, calculating satisfaction. He straightened up with brazen elegance. 

"Well, look, I'm good at reading people. It's my job. It's how I built my empire. And today I saw how hard you tried to defend yourself in the restaurant, I saw the fire in your eyes, but I also saw defeat. If you say you gave up everything for a man, then I assume you're here without a job, without any recognized qualifications in this country, without friends you can trust, and quite possibly, without money... or am I wrong?"

IV 5. In exchange for making my daughter happy.

Zara Fox's POV 

dmn man. He seemed able to see right through me, reading my despair like an open book. 

He was right about everything. 

But what he didn't know was that I always had a plan B. I could go back to London, yes; retrace my steps, lick my wounds in silence, swallow my pride, and beg my father for forgiveness. I knew I would have to endure his eternal "I told you so," like an inevitable sentence… and still, take the risk that his fury would drag him too far, until he became a murderer, capable of taking Henry's life with his own hands. 

But that would mean accepting my failure. 

It would mean being the easiest Fox to deceive, the one who let herself be carried away by an illusion and returned with her tail between her legs. 

No! I had to rebuild myself. Without my father's protection. Without his money. Without his name as a shield. I had to prove to myself, and to him, that I could survive despite everything. 

“I must admit that in your… sociological analysis… you’re not entirely wrong,” I lied, crossing my arms over my chest, trying to hide the trembling of my hands. “But that doesn’t mean I’m desperate. I still have options.” 

“If you say so…” he murmured, picking up his glass again and finishing the rest of the whiskey. His eyes flashed with a glint that told me he was about to make his final offer. “Look, Doctor. I’m offering you a one-year marriage. A year in which you’ll have every perk you could want, plus prestige. If money is your concern, I assure you your bank account will be the last thing on your mind. If you want a job, I can get you a position at the best pediatric hospital in the city with a single phone call. If you want that man’s wife, Henry, to never breathe near you again, I’ll make sure she disappears from your life completely. Ask me for anything you want, as long as you accept.” 

The offer was tempting. More than tempting, it was almost indecent in its generosity. Mainly because it would cleanse my dignity, my reputation. Not be anyone's mistress. Being the wife of a powerful man, even if it was a charade, would give me the time and the shield I needed to rebuild my career and my life. 

The rest—the money, the position at the hospital—I could acquire it myself eventually. But the protection and status he offered were immediate. 

"In exchange for what?" I asked, my voice now firmer, straightening my back and looking him directly in the eyes. There was no trace of Dr. Giraffe in me now. I was Zara Fox, negotiating her future. "What is it that a man like you, who seems to have everything, needs from me?" I didn't buy the story of a simple marriage. 

He paused for a moment before answering. The strategic gleam in his eyes softened slightly, replaced by a shadow of vulnerability that surprised me. The way his voice softened, becoming almost soothing, touched me deeply. 

"In exchange for making my daughter happy." 

My heart skipped a beat. I hadn't expected that. I expected him to ask me to be his trophy at charity dinners, to warm his bed, to be a silent companion. But to make Alina happy? 

"And how do you expect me to do that?" I asked, without thinking, genuine confusion in my voice. "Happiness isn't something you can buy." 

"Doctor… I'm a very realistic man," he said, his tone becoming practical and curt again. "I know forcing you to give Alina genuine affection is impossible. But I can ask you to take care of her. To be a mother to her. To go shopping with her, to take her to school, to tell her those giraffe stories she loved so much in London. One year of being the perfect mother to her. A year of sham marriage, yes, but a year in which my daughter would have a stable mother figure."

I didn't know whether to laugh or cry at the desperate, almost pathetic way in which this man, who seemed to pull the strings in the city, wanted to buy his daughter's happiness. 

His words sounded somewhat unreal, almost fantastical, as if he believed that a wife for hire could heal a child's wounds. But then I remembered little Alina's face in the hospital. Those big blue eyes, like her father's, filled with a silent pain, a loneliness that no amount of toys or luxuries seemed able to fill. 

"Why are you asking this of me?" I asked, my voice now soft. "There must be hundreds of women in this city who would accept this deal without hesitation, just for the money and the status. Why me?" 

He looked at me with brutal honesty. 

"I'll be honest with you, Doctor. In London, I noticed the affinity she showed for you" he paused briefly before continuing "My daughter has a problem: she doesn't speak. She's already been evaluated by the best neurologist and a renowned child psychologist. It's not a physical condition; she's silent by choice. She lives locked in her own world, one made of silence. And today, a doctor repeated something I've been hearing for years: what Alina needs... is a mother."

My heart ached at the image of little Alina locked in her silence, suffering a grief that no one could fully understand. 

As a pediatrician, I had seen many cases of children who reacted to trauma or loss with mutism. It was a defense mechanism, a way to protect themselves from the pain of the outside world. 

"May I ask… where is her mother?" I exclaimed, my voice barely a whisper. I knew I was treading on dangerous ground, but I needed to understand. 

His expression changed instantly. Coldness returned to his face, but this time it was mixed with a contained fury that made me shudder. His eyes became icy blades. 

"She doesn't have a mother," he said, his voice harsh, sharp as glass. 

“We all come from one, sir,” I replied, my voice calm but firm. I wasn’t going to be intimidated by his bad mood. “If we’re going to make a deal, I need honesty. I can’t be a mother to your daughter if I don’t know what happened to the previous one.” 

The look he gave me was almost deadly. I felt he was about to throw me out of his apartment, to cancel the deal before it even began. But I didn’t move. I stood looking at him, holding his gaze with a determination that, for the first time, seemed to surprise him. 

“If you don’t tell me, then I’ll leave…” I said, getting up simply from the sofa, ready to walk out the door and face my fate alone. 

But before I could take a step, I felt his hand close around my wrist. His grip was firm, possessive, but not painful. He pulled me down, silently demanding that I sit back down. His eyes were locked on mine, a battle of wills he clearly wasn't about to lose. 

"Fine," he grunted, releasing my wrist and sitting back down, running a hand through his hair in frustration. His mask of coldness had cracked slightly. "Alina's mother... died when she was born." 

Now I could understand that pain, that despair I saw in his eyes when he spoke of his daughter. He wasn't just a rich father trying to buy an easy solution. He was a broken man, trying to mend what fate had shattered. 

I looked at him with genuine understanding. My heart softened a little toward this arrogant and insufferable man. 

"I'm so sorry for your loss, sir," I said, patting his hand in an instinctive gesture of comfort. "I'm truly sorry. It's a terrible tragedy." 

I quickly withdrew my hand, realizing how bold I'd been. I resumed my professional posture. 

"I... accept the deal. I agree to be Alina's mother for a year. I agree to pretend to have a perfect marriage. But I have my own conditions." 

He looked at me curiously. 

"I'm all ears, Dr. Giraffe..." 

"First, you'll help me hide from my father. I ran away from home in London, and I don't want to go back looking like a loser, much less hear 'I told you so' from him. I want to prove to myself that I can make it on my own, even with a broken heart. You have the power and the resources to make me invisible to him." 

He nodded slowly, a brazen, calculating smile spreading across his face. 

"Don't worry about that," he exclaimed. "If you marry me, you'll take my last name. I assure you, you'll have more prestige and security than you've ever known. Besides," he added, leaning forward, "you won't need to work this year. Not if you don't want to. Believe me, I'll be an excellent provider. Your wish is my command." 

Sexist! The word echoed in my mind. It sounded so easy for a man like him. He believed that with money and power he could buy anything, even my ambitions. 

"Look, sir," I said, my tone icy, crossing my arms again. "I want to resume my medical residency here in New York and finish my specialization in pediatrics. Do you understand? I'm not a trophy to be displayed in a glass case. I'm a professional woman." 

He let out a laugh, a husky, genuine sound that resonated in the luxurious apartment. He leaned back on the sofa, looking at me with a mixture of amusement and a new kind of respect. 

"Well... the little giraffe can be a lioness when she wants to. How interesting," he commented ironically, a flicker of challenge in his eyes. "I like that way of thinking. I don't object, but I should clarify that working with me won't be necessary." 

My eyes narrowed. I didn't like his superior tone. 

"What I'm telling you is true, sir. So don't expect a submissive, kept wife from me. Believe me, your money is the last thing on my mind. I have my own plans." 

He let out another laugh, this time lower, more husky, almost dangerous. He leaned forward once more, his face inches from mine.

"In my world, little lioness..." he said, his voice dropping to a seductive and terrifying whisper, "everyone has a price. Absolutely everyone. It's just a matter of finding the right currency." 

"Not in my case," I replied, my voice firm. "So, if you want this contract, it'll be like this: you give me absolute protection, you help me finish my specialization, and I'll be the best mother Alina could ever wish for. A year of pretense, yes. But a year of professional pretense. Do we have a deal?"

V 6. My Fiancée

Julian Mackenzie's POV 

The giraffe doctor's overly defensive attitude struck me as comical. She was so different from all the women I'd ever met. Not even Lia had that innocent air about her that this woman possessed. 

What she was asking was easy for me. I was even more than willing to lend a hand to make her degree and US residency official. 

"Of course," I said, taking her hand to seal the deal. 

Her smile shifted from sweet to wicked. It was quick, but I noticed. 

"Then it's best if the contract is drawn up, and I request that a few conditions be added." 

Her trying to negotiate with me was even funnier. I could see she had a strong personality, but even when she was angry, she looked like a little lion cub. 

"Fine, you can add your conditions. We'll do that tomorrow in my office. For now, I'll take you to your hotel. You can even stay in this apartment until we get married,” I told her. 

She looked around, not entirely convinced. I didn’t quite understand why she was so analytical, even as soon as she walked in, until she spoke: 

“No, I won’t be staying here.”

 Those were her first words. I didn’t understand why. After all, this apartment was luxurious. Wasn’t she used to luxury? 

“Can I know the reason for your refusal?” 

“Well, I’m not going to stay in a womanizer’s den. God only knows how many women have set foot in this place.” 

I hadn’t expected that reaction, much less the way she said it. It was true that many women had been here, but I didn’t consider myself a womanizer. I had always been upfront about my affairs. 

“Don’t you think this way of criticizing me is very aggressive?” I asked. 

“It’s not criticism, it’s reality. I have a brother, and I know very well what men like him do in places like this. So I won’t be staying here.” 

"It's true, I'm no saint, but I'm not a womanizer either. Fine, if the young lady doesn't want to stay here, we'll find somewhere else to stay." 

"Okay, but I think it would be best if you dropped me off at my hotel. I'm tired; it's been a difficult day." 

"Alright, Dr. Giraffe… I'll take you to your hotel." 

"Zara… my name is Zara, not Dr. Giraffe. Is that clear?" 

I smiled at her words. Zara… it was a name that suited her very well. 

"Okay, Zara. My name is Julian." 

She smiled and said without hesitation: 

"A very nice name for a very cold man," she commented as she stood up and walked toward the door to leave. 

"A very direct woman," I thought. 

I took her to the address she gave me. When I saw the area, I raised my eyebrows. 

“Are you really that short of money that you have to stay in a place like this?” 

She looked back at me and said, “It’s all I can pay in cash. If I use my cards, my father will be able to track me down.” 

She talked so much about her father that I was starting to wonder if he was a possessive, controlling lunatic. 

I parked the car and got out to walk her there. As we entered the lobby, she turned back to me: 

“You can go now, Julián. I can walk from here on my own.” 

“Leave you here? Impossible. From today on, you’re officially my fiancée, and nothing you say will change my mind. You don’t want to stay in my apartment, I accept that, but I’ll put you up in a better hotel.” 

I owned stock in a well-known hotel chain. I wasn’t just a successful lawyer; I also had a couple of other businesses. 

“It’s not necessary,” she replied. 

It wasn’t an option. I didn’t even ask. 

“It’s for your safety. For your peace of mind, I'll reserve it in my name, okay?" 

I was grateful she didn't make it any harder for me… she finally nodded. I took the key from her hand and practically dragged her to her room. She had a small suitcase. 

I took it and we left. 

I had a presidential suite—it was one of the perks for members—and I gave it to her. 

"You'll be more comfortable here, Zara," I said as I left, once she'd settled in. 

"Thank you, Julián," she replied politely. 

We were standing face to face. She was an elegant woman, tall, yes, but even in the heels she was wearing, she didn't reach me. I was 6'3" and she was, at most, 5'9". Her head almost touched my chin. 

"I'll come for you tomorrow. We'll go for breakfast and I'll take you to my office to finalize our agreement." 

"Okay. Get some rest." 

“Do you have a number I can call you on?” I asked. 

“No, my cell phone is off, and I haven’t gotten a new line yet.” 

“Okay. Just don’t move from here. We’ll take care of everything tomorrow.” 

She nodded. I turned around and left. 

I drove straight home. It was very late when I arrived. My father was still waiting for me in the living room. 

“Son, it’s very late.” 

“I know, Dad,” I said, loosening my tie and sighing. “I had a strange day today.” 

“Strange? Why?” 

“Because today, Dad, I found the woman who will be Alina’s mother.”

“What are you talking about?” he asked. 

“That I found her, Dad. I found the perfect woman to be Alina’s mother and my wife.”

"Julian, do you really know what you're talking about?" 

"Yes, Dad. I'm getting married." 

"Julian, marriage isn't a joke. Are you sure? What happened to all those times you told me you didn't believe in love? Son, I don't want you to get hurt like that woman did... Irina." 

The mention of Alina's mother filled me with the same fury I'd felt since she told me she was going to have an abortion. 

Irina Valkova. The woman I buried in my heart, the one who made me stop believing in love. 

I swore I'd never love again. It was pointless. But in my family, love was important, so I wasn't about to tell them that this woman I was marrying was just a well-made arrangement. 

"Dad, that's all in the past. Zara is lovely, and Alina feels comfortable with her." 

"Alina? Has she met her?" he asked. 

“Yes, Dad, and you will too. She’s not from this country; I met her in London. So, in order for her to live here, we’ll have a civil ceremony soon, and the church wedding will be in a year.” 

I lied to him. This was the second lie of the day. Not typical of me. I might be a scoundrel, but never a liar. And today I crossed that line. 

I lied to Zara when I told her Alina’s mother had died, and now to my father, who had always been my confidant, talking about Zara as if I truly loved her. 

“That’s fine, son. From what you’re saying, she’s a very interesting woman.” 

More than interesting, I repeated to myself. 

She’ll be the key to my daughter’s happiness. 

“Yes, Dad. Let’s get some rest.” I escorted him to his room and then sought refuge in my little girl’s. 

She slept in absolute peace, oblivious to the wounds I carry in my soul and the trail of ashes I had to leave behind to have her with me today. 

Because only the day I held her in my arms for the first time—small, fragile, mine—did I feel my heart begin to beat again after so long dormant. 

Now, the path has closed behind me. There is no turning back. I will marry; I will sign a contract, seal a pact, and surrender my freedom for a single purpose: her happiness.

VI 7. Old?

Julian Mackenzie's POV 

The next day, the sun was barely beginning to paint the sky when I was already up. My exercise routine wasn't just for vanity; it was the only way to release the tension built up from what awaited me. 

After a quick shower, I slipped into one of my tailored suits. The cut was perfect, accentuating my shoulders with the precision that only money and good taste can buy. 

In the kitchen, the aroma of coffee and pancakes filled the air as I prepared breakfast for Alina. It's my favorite ritual, the only moment of the day when the world shrinks to my daughter's smile. 

She appears in her school uniform, a whirlwind of energy, and gives me a kiss. Her blue eyes, a carbon copy of mine, shine with that light that only innocence can give. My parents and my grandfather Bruce join us at the table. The smell of home gives me a false sense of peace. 

"Family, I have a surprise. I'm taking you out to dinner tonight. I want you to meet someone very special." 

Alina looks at me curiously, her eyebrows arched in a silent question. 

"Baby, I know you're going to love it," I say, stroking her cheek. "Your grandparents are picking you up today. I have things to do, but I'll see you tonight." 

She nods, reassured, and smiles. 

"Julian, what's this all about?" My mother's voice cuts through the familiar atmosphere, that tone that's known all my lies since I was old enough to understand. 

"Relax, Mom," I say, getting up and straightening my shirt cuffs. "I'll just say that I listened to your advice." 

I wink at her and leave before she can ask any more questions. The echo of her doubts fades as I close the door. 

It's eight in the morning. Zara must be waiting for me.

I arrive at the hotel with an iron will. I order the manager to bring breakfast up to my suite. I don't know her tastes, so I order everything. A calculated excess. This is my territory, and I want her to know it from the first bite. 

I knock on the door. When she opens it, my pulse quickens. It's not a reaction I can control, but one I won't admit aloud either. 

Zara is perfectly dressed. A dress that clings to her curves, her hair pulled back in a ponytail that reveals her neck, elegant and fragile at the same time. 

"Good morning, Zara." 

"Good morning, Julian," her voice is as soft as silk. 

I made my way into the room without waiting for an invitation. Dominating the space was part of my nature. 

"I ordered breakfast. How about we eat and then go to my office?" 

She nods, a minimal but firm movement. However, when the waiter entered with the excessive number of trays, Zara rolled her eyes with an elegance that I found both irritating and fascinating. 

"Don't you think this is an excessive amount of food?" she asked, raising an eyebrow. 

I shrugged, leaning against the window frame to get a better look at her.

"No," I replied, shrugging as I sat down. "I didn't know what you liked, so I ordered everything on the menu." 

I sat down in one of the chairs facing the small table and gestured to the one opposite with a slight nod: an order disguised as an invitation. 

"Come, sit down and enjoy." 

"Thank you," she said, moving with that distinctly British grace. 

She looked young, too young. If I hadn't met her in the hospital, I would have sworn she wasn't even of legal age yet. She has a sweet air about her, yes. But also a quiet determination. 

"Zara." 

"Yes?" 

"How old are you?" Curiosity got the better of me. 

"I recently turned twenty-six. And you?" 

"I'll be thirty-six in two months," I replied, and for the first time in my life, feeling that ten-year age difference weighed heavily on my chest. 

"Wow... you're old," she remarked with a nonchalance that struck a blow to my ego. 

The word stings. No one, absolutely no one, has ever called me old in my life. 

"Old?" I paused before adding, "My father is ten years older than my mother and he's never looked old next to her," I retorted, my voice dropping an octave, laden with that possessive virility. "The men in my family are very... vigorous. My grandfather married my grandmother when he was twenty years older." 

She let out a laugh that broke the tension. 

“You don’t need to explain,” she said, regaining her composure with a speed that made me doubt my own judgment. “In a marriage of convenience, age isn’t important. After all, we’ll be free in a year.” 

dmn it, she was right. Why was I justifying my age? 

“That’s true. So, if you’re finished, let’s go. We have a lot to do,” I said, regaining my composure. 

We arrived at my office in record time. My secretary, a woman I trusted completely, who had seen me climb every rung of my career as a lawyer, greeted us with a surprised smile at seeing me accompanied, since I've never brought a woman here who isn't a family member.

I gestured for Zara to take a seat in the chair across from my mahogany desk, while I sank into my leather armchair, reclaiming my territory. 

Susan looked at us, bewildered; I suppose that seeing Zara, a complete stranger, sitting across from my desk as if she were born to be there, must feel like the end of the world. 

"Susan, no one is to interrupt us," I ordered. 

She nodded and left. 

"Let's clarify the terms," ​​I began, crossing my fingers on the desk. "I've drafted the basic clauses, but I want to add a crucial one: if my daughter shows the slightest sign of discomfort with you, the contract is null and void. Immediate divorce, regardless of how much time has passed." I exclaimed, making it clear that my daughter was untouchable. 

"I understand," Zara replied, unfazed. "That sounds perfect. But I also have a couple of clauses to add." 

I look at her with a wry smile. So now the giraffe doctor has demands? 

"Go ahead," I replied, leaning back in my chair, expecting some absurd financial request. 

Forgetting that Zara wasn't like the others. 

She leans slightly forward, and suddenly the air in the office becomes thick. 

"Julian, marriage is a serious commitment. Even if it's by contract, I want it to be handled with seriousness. Number one: we're going to make it a rule that, at least three nights a week, you have dinner with Alina and me. You'll also be obligated to take us on a trip once a month. My father, no matter how much work he had, was always there for us, and we were his priority. I want to give your daughter that example, the same one I grew up with." 

I remain silent, assessing her. It's not a request. It's a sentence. 

“Number two,” she continued, her voice firm, “as your wife, you will respect my place both in public and in private. And by that, I mean you will commit to being faithful to this contract and the marriage bond we are about to enter into. You understand, right? That your ‘nighttime adventures’ end for the duration of our marriage?” 

My blood boils, but not with anger. With disbelief. Does this little girl intend to set limits for me? 

I lean forward, resting my elbows on the desk, my gaze hardening. 

“I understand the fidelity,” I said, my voice a low whisper. “But I will add a condition. You will fulfill your role as a wife. Both in public… and in private.”
